notes:
I found notes for every verse. A few gaps first:

- **No sources found:** Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Orthodox (oca.org), bibleodyssey.org, and any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Those are left out.
- **NET notes:** I only saw them as quoted on preceptaustin.org, not on netbible.org itself.
- **Traditions:** Among the Protestant sources I read, I found no real disagreement about what the chapter means. The main split I found is Protestant vs. Catholic over monastic vows (v. 2–5). The other debates are between individual commentators, not traditions.

---

## v. 1

- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says Moses gave this to the tribal leaders so they could pass it on to the rest of Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-30/
- **Older-critical view:** The Pulpit Commentary notes that only this passage says a law went to the "heads of the tribes." It says this suggests that this chapter was inserted either by some other hand or from a different source. It also treats this chapter and Leviticus 27 as two separate pieces of law about the same subject. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/30.htm

## v. 2

- **Two kinds of vow:** Ellicott says the verse names two kinds. The *neder* is a positive vow, or vow of performance (a promise to do something). The *issar* is a negative vow, or a vow of abstinence (a promise to go without something). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-30.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary qualifies this: the Nazirite vow was a *neder* yet was a vow of abstinence, so the distinction isn't strict. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/30.htm
- **Keeping your word:** Ellicott says the verse warns that it was better for them not to vow than to vow and not to pay. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-30.html
  - Poole (quoted on Biblehub) says "break" literally means "profane." Breaking a vow would make a person's word profane, or vile and contemptible in the eyes of others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/30-2.htm
- **Unlawful vows don't bind:** Matthew Henry's Concise: No man can be bound by his own promise to do what he is already, by the Divine precept, forbidden to do. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/30-2.htm
- **Gill (Baptist):** He cites Jewish teaching that a valid vow required a minimum age (13, per the Targum). He rejects the rabbinic idea that a court or wise man could release a man from his vow, calling it a tradition that makes void God's command. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/30-2.html
- **Guzik (enduringword.com):** He says Matthew 5:34–37 is about honesty, not a ban on all oaths, since God, Jesus and Paul all swore oaths. He calls broken vows an overlooked sin. He quotes Trapp that God alone is the proper object of a vow, so vowing to angels or saints is idolatry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-30/
- **Reformed (Westminster Confession 22):** A vow is of the like nature with a promissory oath, and ought to be made with the like religious care, and to be performed with the like faithfulness. A vow cannot oblige a person to sin. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/westminster-confession-faith
  - A Ligonier devotional uses Num 30:1–2 against first-century rabbinic loopholes that allowed vows not made in God's name to be broken. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jesus-teaching-on-oaths
- **Where Protestants and Catholics differ:** The Baptist Confession (on ccel.org) says vows are to be made to God alone. It calls Popish Monastical Vows, (i) of perpetual single life, professed (k) poverty, and regular obedience "superstitious, and sinful snares." https://www.ccel.org/creeds/bcf/bcfc23.htm
  - Aquinas, by contrast, uses this chapter in his treatment of vows, including vows to enter religious life (see v. 3–5).

## v. 3–5

- **Traditional reading:** The Pulpit Commentary says the daughter had no property of her own, and whose personal services were due to her father. The father's veto has to be spoken aloud, not just thought. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/30.htm
  - Garner-Howes (Baptist) gives the same reasons. It adds that if the father cancels the vow, the responsibility becomes his. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-30.html
- **"On the day he hears":** Wesley (Methodist) says the father must act Speedily, or without delay, allowing only convenient time for deliberation. The time counts from when he learns of the vow, not from when she made it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/30.htm
- **Women could vow:** Guzik notes it was significant that young women could make vows and deal with God directly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-30/
- **"The LORD will absolve her":** F. B. Meyer (quoted on preceptaustin.org): God would not keep her to a promise which was hindered from execution by causes over which she had no control. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-30-commentary
- **NET note on "stand":** The vow becomes a genuine oath through the father's approval, or simply his silence. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-30-commentary
- **Constable:** A daughter's duty to obey her father mattered more than a vow she had chosen to take on herself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/30-9.html
- **"In her youth" (Whedon):** This means youth, not childhood. He cites rabbinic age limits for testing vows. He says father and daughter are "one in responsibility." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-30.html
- **Catholic (Aquinas):** He cites this passage to show that a person under another's authority is not bound by a vow unless that person consents. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3088.htm
  - Elsewhere he applies it to children vowing to enter religious life: a father may cancel or approve such vows. He adds that the girl does not sin by vowing; she binds herself as far as she can without overriding her parents' authority. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3189.htm
  - He also uses the passage for oaths: a superior may cancel an oath on matters under his authority, as a father may cancel his daughter's. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3089.htm

## v. 6–8

- **Debate: betrothed or married?**
  - The Speaker's Commentary (quoted in the Preacher's Homiletical) says the wording points to the case of a girl betrothed, but not yet actually married. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-30.html
  - Whedon agrees: during the betrothal period, control of her vows passed from her father to her husband. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-30.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary says there was little legal difference between married and betrothed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/30.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch and Guzik read it as a vow she made before marriage and brought along with her ( עליה , "upon herself") into her marriage. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/30-13.html
- **Why the husband can cancel:** Pulpit says that otherwise he might suffer loss through an act of which he had no notice. It translates the phrase as "the rash utterance of her lips." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/30.htm
- **A protection for her too:** Allen (quoted on preceptaustin.org) calls this a protective clause, since she might have been pressured into a vow that was not in her best interest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-30-commentary
- **Henry (Presbyterian):** If the husband cancels it, her duty to him takes priority. Keeping the vow would then be disobedience, and she may need forgiveness because perhaps she should have asked his consent first. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_030.cfm

## v. 9

- **Traditional reading:** Widows and divorced women answer directly to God, so no one else can cancel their vows (Constable). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/30-9.html
  - Cole (quoted by Guzik) says such a woman had the same status as a man regarding vows.
  - Allen (also quoted by Guzik) argues the verse shows a divorced woman was truly independent. It counts against the claim that biblical divorce was only a legal fiction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-30/
- **Earlier cancellations stay cancelled:** Henry says a vow her husband cancelled during the marriage does not come back into force when she is widowed or divorced. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_030.cfm
  - Garner-Howes says a vow she made while still married follows the husband's rules. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-30.html
- **Pulpit:** This verse isn't really one of the chapter's cases. It just shows that such women come under the general rule of v. 2. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/30.htm

## v. 10–12

- **Pulpit:** This is the third case, a wife living with her husband. The husband has the same authority as a father, but his responsibility is stated more strongly because he is more closely involved in her affairs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/30.htm
- **Guzik:** Verses 6–8 cover vows a woman brought into marriage. Verses 10–15 cover vows made during marriage. He quotes Cole that Hannah's vow (1 Samuel 1) is an example: her husband Elkanah let it stand by doing nothing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-30/
- **The Expositor's Bible (Watson):** The key point is that no intrusion of the priest is permitted. If the "Priests' Code" had been meant to set up rule by priests, this would have been the chance to bring priestly influence into family life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-30.html

## v. 13

- **"To deny herself" / "afflict her soul":** Wesley explains it as Herself by fasting, by watching, or the like. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/30.htm
  - Pulpit links the phrase to the Day of Atonement fast and to 1 Corinthians 7:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/30.htm
- **NET note:** The vow might involve abstaining from things, perhaps even sexual relations within marriage. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-30-commentary
- **Gill:** The husband's power was meant to prevent confusion in the home and spending he couldn't afford. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/numbers/30-13.html
- **Biblehub Study Bible:** The husband's leadership is meant for protection and order, not domination. https://biblehub.com/numbers/30-13.htm
- **Catholic translations:** The Douay-Rheims spells out "by fasting, or abstinence from other things." https://biblehub.com/numbers/30-13.htm

## v. 14

- **Traditional reading:** Silence confirms the vow. Whedon says the husband's power to cancel ended after the day he heard of it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-30.html
- **Expositor's Bible:** Even if the vow costs the family money or inconvenience, by staying silent the head of the house has bound himself to it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-30.html

## v. 15

- **Majority view:** If the husband stays silent at first but later stops her, the guilt is his.
  - Wesley: her non - performance of her vow shall be imputed to him, not to her. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/numbers/30.htm
  - Pulpit says the same and points to Leviticus 5 for how that guilt was atoned for. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/30.htm
  - Gill adds that a late cancellation might come from a spirit of contradiction or greed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/30-15.htm
  - Whedon says a sin offering had to be brought. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-30.html
- **Henry's wider reading:** If what she vowed was truly good and he cancelled it out of covetousness, or humour, or to show his authority, he will have much to answer for, even though she is released. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_030.cfm
- **Other readings** (from the Spanish-language page on StudyLight):
  - Pett gives both views. He prefers reading the verse as a general warning not to cancel a wife's vow lightly.
  - Coke notes that Houbigant, following the Samaritan text and the Septuagint, translates "he shall bear his own iniquity." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/30-15.html

## v. 16

- **G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Guzik):** The rules show God's concern for family unity. In no family must there be two supreme authorities. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-30/
- **Biblehub summary:** The verse reflects Israel's tribal, patriarchal society and shows how personal devotion to God fits with authority in the household. https://biblehub.com/numbers/30.htm
- **Expositor's Bible application:** It is an abuse for the church to get promises from women without the knowledge of those closest to them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-30.html
